subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 24-year-old woman has 4 days of sharp left-sided chest pain that changes with body position and worsens with deep inspiration. She points with one finger to a tender spot at the costochondral junction. ECG and troponin are normal, and she has no dyspnea or fever.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Costochondritis is inflammation of the costochondral or costosternal junctions and presents with focal tenderness to palpation and sharp, positional chest pain that may worsen with deep inspiration. It is more common in younger female patients and can mimic myocardial infarction or pulmonary embolism. Normal cardiac studies and reproducible chest wall tenderness support the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Myocardial infarction causes pressure-like pain without focal chest wall tenderness and would show ischemic ECG changes or elevated troponin.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pulmonary embolism produces pleuritic pain and dyspnea with tachycardia but not focal reproducible tenderness at a costochondral junction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pericarditis causes positional pain relieved by leaning forward with a friction rub and diffuse ECG changes rather than a single tender costochondral point.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain with fever and a positive Murphy sign, not sharp positional anterior chest wall pain in a young woman.

educationalObjective: Costochondritis causes focal costochondral tenderness and sharp positional chest pain in younger women, mimicking cardiac or pulmonary disease.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Pathology: Common musculoskeletal overuse conditions

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 32-year-old woman who recently gave birth has radial-sided wrist pain that worsens when she lifts her baby. Tenderness is maximal over the radial styloid, and pain is reproduced by passive ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb held in flexion (positive Finkelstein test).
question: Which tendons are affected in this condition?

options.text: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Extensor pollicis longus and abductor digiti minimi

explanation_correct: De Quervain tenosynovitis is noninflammatory thickening of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons, causing pain and tenderness at the radial styloid. A positive Finkelstein test reproduces the pain with stretching of these thumb tendons. Risk is increased in new mothers lifting babies, golfers, racquet sport players, and thumb texters.

explanation_incorrect.A: The extensor carpi radialis tendons cross the wrist but are not the involved tendons in de Quervain tenosynovitis and are not tested by the Finkelstein maneuver.
explanation_incorrect.B: Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus are volar wrist flexors; de Quervain involves the dorsal first extensor compartment thumb tendons.
explanation_incorrect.D: Extensor pollicis longus lies in the third extensor compartment and abductor digiti minimi is hypothenar; neither is the pair affected in de Quervain.
explanation_incorrect.E: Brachioradialis and pronator teres are forearm muscles acting at the elbow and proximal forearm, not the radial styloid tendons.

educationalObjective: De Quervain tenosynovitis affects the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid with a positive Finkelstein test.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 62-year-old man of Northern European descent has noticed a painless progressive bending contracture of the ring and little fingers of both hands over 2 years. Examination reveals thick cords in the superficial palmar fascia and inability to fully extend the affected digits. There is no sensory loss or wrist swelling.
question: Which of the following best describes this condition?

options.text: Mucin-filled ganglion cyst of the dorsal wrist
Median nerve entrapment at the carpal tunnel
Stenosing tenosynovitis of the flexor tendon (trigger finger)
Fibroblastic proliferation of the superficial palmar fascia
Noninflammatory thickening of the abductor pollicis longus tendon

explanation_correct: Dupuytren contracture is caused by fibroblastic proliferation and thickening of the superficial palmar fascia, typically involving the fascia at the base of the ring and little fingers. The etiology is unknown, and it is most frequent in males older than 50 of Northern European descent. The painless flexion contracture and palpable palmar cords are characteristic.

explanation_incorrect.A: A ganglion cyst is a mucin-filled, transilluminating dorsal wrist swelling that usually resolves spontaneously; it does not produce digital flexion contractures.
explanation_incorrect.B: Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median-distribution paresthesias and thenar atrophy, not painless palmar cords and finger contractures.
explanation_incorrect.C: Trigger finger causes painful catching or locking of a single digit from flexor tendon stenosing tenosynovitis, not bilateral painless palmar fascial cords.
explanation_incorrect.E: De Quervain tenosynovitis affects the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid and produces radial wrist pain, not ring and little finger contractures.

educationalObjective: Dupuytren contracture is fibroblastic thickening of the superficial palmar fascia causing ring and little finger flexion contracture in older Northern European males.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 28-year-old woman notices a smooth, painless swelling on the dorsal aspect of her wrist that appeared over several weeks. It is cystic and transilluminates when a penlight is applied. There is no redness, warmth, or limitation of motion, and she asks whether it will disappear on its own.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: A ganglion cyst is a mucin-filled swelling overlying a joint or tendon sheath, most commonly on the dorsal side of the wrist. It characteristically transilluminates with light, whereas tumors do not, and it usually resolves spontaneously. The painless dorsal wrist location and transillumination make this the most likely diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: An epidermoid inclusion cyst contains keratinous debris, is not typically transilluminating, and is not the classic dorsal wrist lesion arising from a joint or tendon sheath.
explanation_incorrect.B: A lipoma is a soft, doughy subcutaneous mass that does not transilluminate and is not specifically associated with the dorsal wrist joint or tendon sheath.
explanation_incorrect.C: A gouty tophus is a firm, often erythematous deposit of urate crystals with associated arthritis, not a translucent cystic dorsal wrist swelling.
explanation_incorrect.D: Synovial sarcoma is a malignant soft tissue tumor that would not transilluminate and would typically be firm, progressive, and potentially symptomatic.

educationalObjective: A dorsal wrist ganglion cyst is mucin-filled and transilluminates, distinguishing it from solid tumors, and often resolves spontaneously.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 30-year-old long-distance runner recently increased her weekly mileage and now has a burning pain on the lateral aspect of her knee that appears toward the end of runs. Tenderness is elicited over the lateral femoral epicondyle, and there is no joint effusion or meniscal click on testing.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Iliotibial band syndrome is an overuse injury of the lateral knee occurring primarily in runners. Pain develops from friction of the iliotibial band against the lateral femoral epicondyle, typically after an increase in training load. Lateral knee pain with tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and no effusion fits this diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Prepatellar bursitis causes anterior knee swelling from kneeling, not exertional lateral knee pain over the lateral femoral epicondyle.
explanation_incorrect.C: A popliteal cyst produces posterior knee swelling associated with chronic joint disease, not lateral exertional pain in a runner.
explanation_incorrect.D: A lateral meniscus tear usually follows a twisting injury with mechanical locking or joint-line tenderness and effusion, not friction-related lateral epicondylar pain.
explanation_incorrect.E: Patellofemoral syndrome causes anterior knee pain worse with prolonged sitting or flexed-knee weight bearing, not lateral friction pain.

educationalObjective: Iliotibial band syndrome causes lateral knee pain in runners from friction of the band against the lateral femoral epicondyle.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Pathology: Common musculoskeletal overuse conditions

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 25-year-old man sustains a closed tibial shaft fracture in a motorcycle crash. Over the next several hours he develops severe pain out of proportion to his injury, tense swelling of the calf, and pain on passive stretch of the toes. He becomes progressively paresthetic. CT angiography shows patent arteries. Serum creatine kinase is elevated.
question: Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism of this condition?

options.text: Acute arterial transection producing immediate pulselessness and pallor
Increased fascial compartment pressure causing venous outflow obstruction, arteriolar collapse, and muscle anoxia
Deep vein thrombosis causing venous congestion and secondary arterial spasm
Crystal deposition in the joint triggering acute inflammatory arthritis
Bacterial invasion of muscle with localized pus and systemic sepsis

explanation_correct: Limb compartment syndrome results from increased pressure within a fascial compartment, causing venous outflow obstruction and arteriolar collapse, which lead to anoxia, necrosis, rhabdomyolysis, and potentially acute tubular necrosis. Long bone fractures such as tibia fractures, reperfusion injury, and animal venoms are causes. Severe pain, tense compartments, and pain with passive stretch are early; elevated creatine kinase and motor deficits are late signs of irreversible damage.

explanation_incorrect.A: Arterial transection would cause immediate pulselessness and pallor; in compartment syndrome pulses are often palpable until late and the primary problem is microcirculatory collapse.
explanation_incorrect.C: Deep vein thrombosis does not produce tense fascial compartments with pain on passive stretch and the 5 P's of compartment syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Crystal deposition causes gout or pseudogout with joint inflammation, not post-traumatic compartment pressure elevation and rhabdomyolysis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Necrotizing infection can mimic compartment syndrome but does not arise from a closed tibial fracture with intact overlying skin and patent arteries in this manner.

educationalObjective: Compartment syndrome is rising fascial pressure causing venous outflow obstruction and muscle anoxia; pain with passive stretch is early, while CK rise and deficits are late.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 19-year-old military recruit develops diffuse pain and tenderness along the medial border of both shins after 2 weeks of intense marching. Radiographs show no cortical breach or periosteal reaction. Her clinician attributes the symptoms to bone remodeling imbalance in the tibial cortex.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tibial stress fracture with a visible cortical break

explanation_correct: Medial tibial stress syndrome, or shin splints, is a common cause of shin pain and diffuse tenderness in runners and military recruits. It is caused by bone resorption that outpaces bone formation in the tibial cortex. The diffuse tenderness and absence of a focal cortical breach or compartment signs support the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: A stress fracture would show a focal cortical breach or periosteal reaction on imaging and more localized bony tenderness rather than diffuse shin pain.
explanation_incorrect.B: Compartment syndrome produces tense swelling and pain with passive stretch, not the diffuse activity-related shin tenderness described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Plantar fasciitis causes heel pain worse with first steps in the morning, not shin pain in a marching recruit.
explanation_incorrect.E: Achilles tendinopathy causes posterior ankle and heel cord pain and swelling, not diffuse medial tibial tenderness.

educationalObjective: Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints) is diffuse shin pain in runners and recruits caused by resorption exceeding bone formation.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 50-year-old woman with obesity and flat feet has 6 weeks of heel pain that is worst with her first steps in the morning and improves after walking for a while. Tenderness is present at the plantar aspect of the heel, and a lateral radiograph shows a small calcaneal spur.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the plantar aponeurosis characterized by heel pain that is worse with the first steps in the morning or after inactivity, with plantar heel tenderness. It is associated with obesity, prolonged standing or jumping, and flat feet, and heel spurs often coexist. This patient's presentation is classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: A calcaneal stress fracture causes focal bony tenderness and pain that worsens with weight bearing and persists rather than classically improving after initial morning steps.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tarsal tunnel syndrome compresses the posterior tibial nerve and causes burning paresthesias in the sole, not localized plantar heel tenderness with morning stiffness.
explanation_incorrect.C: Achilles tendinopathy produces pain and thickening of the heel cord above the calcaneus, not plantar heel pain with first steps.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gouty arthritis would present with acute redness, warmth, and severe pain of a joint, not chronic mechanical plantar heel pain with a spur.

educationalObjective: Plantar fasciitis causes plantar heel pain worse with first morning steps, associated with obesity, prolonged standing, and flat feet, often with heel spurs.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Pathology: Common musculoskeletal overuse conditions

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 34-year-old woman has 3 months of dull, constant right-sided facial pain that worsens with jaw movement and chewing. She also has intermittent ear pain and headache, and she cannot open her mouth fully. Sinus CT is normal, dental examination is unremarkable, and there is no scalp tenderness or vision change.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Temporomandibular disorders involve the temporomandibular joint and muscles of mastication and are multifactorial, associated with TMJ trauma, poor head and neck posture, abnormal trigeminal pain processing, and psychological factors. They produce dull, constant unilateral facial pain that worsens with jaw movement, along with otalgia, headache, and limited range of motion. This matches the patient's presentation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Trigeminal neuralgia produces brief, stabbing, electric-like paroxysms triggered by light touch rather than constant dull pain with jaw movement and limited opening.
explanation_incorrect.B: Sinusitis would show sinus opacification on CT and facial pressure with nasal symptoms, not pain reproducibly worsened by jaw movement with a normal sinus CT.
explanation_incorrect.C: Dental pulpitis would produce localized tooth pain with a dental source on examination, which was unremarkable in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.D: Giant cell arteritis causes scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms in older patients, not chronic unilateral TMJ pain with limited mouth opening.

educationalObjective: Temporomandibular disorder causes dull unilateral facial pain worsened by jaw movement with otalgia, headache, and limited mouth opening.
